candidates.description: CEO pay decreases 17% more in firms with noncompliant boards (majority non-independent directors) than in firms with compliant boards (majority independent directors)
candidates.citation_sentence: Chhaochharia and Grinstein (2009) (henceforth CG) use firms' compliance status before the rule change to identify the causal effect of board composition on CEO pay.
candidates.notes: The replication finds CG's main board independence result is driven by two outlier firms (Apple and Fossil). After excluding them, the effect drops by 74% and becomes statistically indistinguishable from zero. [ling26: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.description: The effect of board independence on CEO pay is moderated by the presence of blockholder directors (nonemployee directors owning 5%+ of shares)
candidates.citation_sentence: Column (1) in panel A of Table III reproduces CG's main result on block ownership from table VII, column (1) of the published paper
candidates.notes: The replication finds CG's blockholder moderation result is also driven by the same outliers (Apple and Fossil). After excluding them, the noncompliance effect for firms without blockholders drops from -0.270 to -0.100 and becomes marginally significant. [ling26: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.description: The effect of board independence on CEO pay varies with institutional ownership concentration (top vs. bottom quartiles)
candidates.citation_sentence: Column (1) in panel B of Table III reproduces CG's results on institutional ownership concentration from Table VII, column (2) of the published paper.
candidates.notes: The replication finds CG's institutional concentration results are also driven by outliers. After excluding Apple and Fossil, neither high nor low institutional concentration groups show significant noncompliance effects. [ling26: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.description: Compensation committee independence requirement does not significantly affect CEO pay
candidates.citation_sentence: Column (1) of Table IV reproduces CG's main result from Table II, column (2) of the published paper
candidates.notes: CG found a null effect of compensation committee noncompliance on CEO pay (coefficient -0.014, p=0.83). The replication also finds null in the full sample (coefficient -0.000), but after excluding outliers the effect reverses to positive and significant (coefficient 0.069, p=0.023). A second coder might code this as 'failure' (null is fragile) or 'inconclusive' (full sample matches but outlier-adjusted result differs). [ling26: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.description: The requirement for fully independent compensation committees decreases CEO pay in noncompliant firms relative to compliant firms.
candidates.citation_sentence: To test prediction, Chhaochharia and Grinstein (2009) (henceforth CG) use firms' compliance status before the rule change to identify the causal effect of board composition on CEO pay.
candidates.notes: After excluding the outliers, the replication finds a statistically significant increase in CEO pay for compensation-committee-noncompliant firms, which the authors describe as an unintended or perverse consequence contrary to the predicted pay reduction.

candidates.description: The NYSE/Nasdaq board-independence requirement causes CEO pay to decrease more in noncompliant firms than in compliant firms.
candidates.citation_sentence: To test prediction, Chhaochharia and Grinstein (2009) (henceforth CG) use firms' compliance status before the rule change to identify the causal effect of board composition on CEO pay.
candidates.notes: The authors state that the original board-independence finding is fragile and driven by Apple and Fossil; excluding these outliers eliminates the effect. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.description: The negative effect of board noncompliance on CEO pay is concentrated in firms without nonemployee blockholder directors, while blockholder directors mute the effect.
candidates.citation_sentence: To test prediction, Chhaochharia and Grinstein (2009) (henceforth CG) use firms' compliance status before the rule change to identify the causal effect of board composition on CEO pay.
candidates.notes: The replication finds a significant decrease for firms without blockholder directors but also a significant increase for firms with blockholder directors, producing mixed moderator-specific results. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.description: The negative effect of board noncompliance on CEO pay is stronger among firms with low institutional ownership concentration than among firms with high concentration.
candidates.citation_sentence: To test prediction, Chhaochharia and Grinstein (2009) (henceforth CG) use firms' compliance status before the rule change to identify the causal effect of board composition on CEO pay.
candidates.notes: The authors report no support for a board-independence-related decrease in CEO pay among firms with either low or high institutional ownership concentration. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]
